topic: std::forward Failure: Incorrect Context for Conditional Casting
explanation: Assumption: `std::forward` guarantees perfect forwarding simply by being present in the function body, regardless of how it is templated or used. Reality: `std::forward<T>(param)` only casts `param` to an rvalue reference (thus enabling a move) if and only if the explicitly specified template argument `T` is an rvalue reference type (i.e., `Widget&&`). If `T` is deduced or specified as a plain value type (`Widget`) or an lvalue reference (`Widget&`), `std::forward` maintains the lvalue classification of the parameter, resulting in a copy. Why It Fails: Perfect forwarding relies on the conditional nature of the cast provided by `std::forward` and the complex rules of universal reference deduction (Item 24). Incorrectly providing the template argument `T` (e.g., forgetting the reference qualification, or forcing it into a non-templated context) prevents the necessary conditional rvalue cast from occurring when it should, leading to unwanted copies or incorrect overload resolution.
practical_example: A developer attempts to simplify the forwarding wrapper by manually applying `std::remove_reference` before forwarding, inadvertently disabling the mechanism required to cast rvalues, causing unnecessary copies throughout the system.
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
